title: Rolex Day-Date Ref. 18038 - 'Burlwood' Dial
description: When the Day-Date was released in 1956, Rolex had made numerous attempts to capture the market with more complicated timepieces such as the Ref. 6036, the Ref. 8171, and the Ref. 6062, but it seemed like buyers were not particularly fond of complicated Rolexes. All of that changed when President Lyndon B. Johnson was spotted wearing one Rolex in particular: a Day-Date. The model has since become known worldwide as ‘The President’ and as a symbol of success and prestige. Simply put, this one stuck. The Day-Date was available for many years on a leather strap with a matching gold buckle, but also on a solid gold bracelet (called a 'President' bracelet), like the example that we have here. However, this isn't your run of the mill Day-Date... Dating to circa 1982, the Reference 18038 that we have here features a special lacquered wood dial. During this time, there where a few different wood dial variants available, with the example that we have here being of the walnut variant. It remains in excellent overall condition, with a smooth glossy surface and clear gold printing throughout. It has applied indices, framed day and date apertures, an applied logo at the 12 o'clock position, and a matching handset. The case, bracelet and bezel are also in strong condition overall, having been lightly previously polished in the past and showing normal signs of wear throughout. Additionally, this piece features the almost magical 'quickset' movement function for setting the date. A real treat if you have ever owned a 4-digit Day-Date! The combination of the brown wood dial within the yellow gold case is undeniably a very of-it's-time combination... We think it had aged beautifully and collectors seem to agree. As a result, these remain sought after and collectible — and its not everyday that they surface in condition like this.

title: Rolex GMT-Master Date Ref. 16758 - Black 'Nipple' Dial
description: The Rolex GMT-Master is one of the most historic and iconic watches the brand ever produced. Its origin dates back to a commission request by Pan American World Airways in the early 50’s for their fleet of pilots who needed access to different time zones. These pieces would feature a similar design to another watch that Rolex was developing around that time, the Submariner, but would include a fourth hand running on 24-hr time, and a bi-colored bezel insert to represent AM/PM times. Those colors, naturally, would be the PanAm colors: Red & Blue. Thus, in 1953, the Ref. 6542 GMT-Master was born. These early pieces were ultimately, fragile arguably flawed in some ways, and were therefor succeeded by the updated Reference 1675 in 1959. Like many Rolex models, the 1675 underwent many small changes over its 21-year production run, with a slew of dial, bezel, bracelet, and hand variations, and would eventually evolve into the 5-digit GMT-Master and GMT-Master IIs. Enter the Reference 16758. These pieces carry over a very similar brown 'nipple' dial and brown bezel insert, while also upgrading the movement with a quickset date function, as well as increased water resistance by way of a sapphire crystal and case redesign. The example that we have here dates to circa 1980 and comes to us in excellent overall condition. The case retains tick and symmetrical lugs at each corner, with those gorgeous factory chamfers clearly visible. It shows normal signs of wear throughout with no damage or blemishes of note. The bezel shows normal wear and retains nice definition and houses an black 24-hr bezel. The matte black dial inside features applied 'nipple' indices filled with Tritium, which show even patina throughout with a beautifully matching handset. This piece comes fitted to a matching, albeit later yellow gold 'rivet' Oyster bracelet with a signed adjustable blade-style clasp. Solid gold sports watches present great value next to their steel siblings... This strong example in particular even a greater value play.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava Ref. 96 - Silver 'Sigma' Dial
description: The Patek Philippe Calatrava. Arguably the brands most iconic model line, and purest expression of the brand. Their raison d'etre if you will. The line has been a hit since its debut in 1932. So much so, that the name "Calatrava" itself has become something of a byword within the watch industry for traditionally styled, no-frills dress watches that simply tell the time. Over the course of its nearly 100-years of production, there have been seemingly countless iterations within the line, with variations in the metal they are made in, with their size, dial configurations, and eventually, complications. The Calatrava that we have here is perhaps the quintessential vintage Calatrava reference: the Reference 96. Coming in at approximately 30.5mm in diameter, this example dates to circa 1940 and is executed in yellow gold. The case itself is healthy and retains symmetrical lugs at all four corners, with a hallmark present on the left case profile and a gently 'rosy' oxidation developing throughout. It presents nicely shows normal signs of wear from age. Inside, the brushed silver dial is a later service unit, featuring 'Sigmas' at the 6 o'clock position, applied 'flat'-style indices, a 'concentric' subsidiary seconds register at the 6 o'clock position, and a matching yellow gold 'feuille' handset. The word icon gets thrown around a lot in the world of watches and horology... this one is absolutely worthy of it. There are watches, and then there are watches! This is one of the latter.

title: Rolex Daytona Ref. 6263 - Matte Black 'Sigma' Dial
description: The Rolex Daytona model, since its initial release, has been at the forefront of the market as the most desirable chronograph in production, and of almost any vintage. Early Daytona’s in particular can be a lot of fun to collect not just because of the recognition they have these days, but also, as with so many other Rolex models early in their life-cycles, because of how many subtle changes they underwent in the fist decade or so, resulting in a plethora of nuanced configurations. One element that was shared throughout the model family, however, was the movement. Prior to the introduction of the automatic-winding Daytonas beginning in circa 1988, all previous Rolex chronographs had been manually-wound, and anything with "Daytona" on the dial, powered by a modified version of Valjoux's highly respected and now very desirable, Calibre 72. The piece that we have here, a Reference 6263, dates to circa 1974 comes to us in excellent overall condition. The 37mm case shows signs of having been very lightly, yet tastefully previously polished, retaining correct proportions and finishing where appropriate. The correct bezel assembly houses a correct 'MK1' black acrylic insert, both of which show normal signs of wear that matches the case. The screw-down pushers are correct 'MK2' units and of course have a screw-down crown between them. Inside, the matte black dial features a pair of 'Sigmas' flanking the Tritium text at the 6 o'clock position, which is correct for this era. The surface remains nice and clean with minimal aging within the 'concentric' silver subsidiary registers, which of course lend themselves to that highly desirable contrast that we love about 'reverse-panda' dials. The Tritium plots exhibit a light and even patina throughout, with only partial loss at a few positions, and a beautifully matching handset. Last but not least, this piece comes fitted to a period-correct Oyster bracelet with a signed blade clasp. Its hard to say more said about vintage Daytonas that hasn't already been said over and over... They are highly collectible, beautiful to behold, and of course, functional and robust watches to wear. This is an excellent, well-rounded example and we're certain its next owner will agree.

title: Breitling Premier Ref. 777 - Silver Dial w/ Portuguese Hallmark
description: Breitling has a long and rich history in chronographs — with an emphasis on aviation chronographs. And like so many other brands who have a watch model, or family that has become synonymous with the brand name itself, the Navitimer is just that for Breitling. As a result, the Navitimer casts a substantial shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the SuperOcean, Top Time, and lesser-known pieces that pre-date model ranges all together. The example that we have here is one of the latter: A chronograph from the Premier family dating to circa 1951. Offered in phenomenal overall condition, this piece possesses many of the hallmark design characteristics found in both vintage Breitling chronographs as well as a handful of other stunning chronographs from this era. The stainless steel case comes in at 37mm in diameter, with attractive, downward curving lugs, 'pump' pushers, a screw-down caseback, and a 'stepped' bezel. It shows only light signs of wear with nice, defined finishing present throughout and a rare hallmark found only on watches imported to Portugal in a certain era on the upper left lug. The dial is simply gorgeous. Wonderfully preserved, the silver surface features a gently 'brushed' finishing along with excellent printed scales, 'concentric' subsidiary registers, and beautifully patinated 'Arabic' numerals with a blued-steel 'syringe' handset tying it all together. It is powered by a manual-winding Calibre 175 from Venus. Vintage chronographs in condition like this, from any brand, are elusive. Collectors tend to hold onto fantastic examples like this one regardless of brand, making this a great opportunity to secure one with a desirable size like this.

title: Ulysse Nardin Monopusher Chronograph - White 'Porcelain' Dial w/ Box & Papers
description: Ulysse Nardin was founded in 1846 by its namesake, a twenty-three-year-old watchmaker who set up shop in Le Locle, Switzerland. From the very beginning, Nardin was interested in producing high-functioning instruments that could be trusted at sea. That focus on precision soon turned the company into a quiet powerhouse among navigators. The marine chronometer became the brand's calling card, and it proved to be a serious business. Ulysse Nardin's chronometers were adopted by more than fifty navies around the world, and the company collected award after award for accuracy along the way. By the late nineteenth century, the name was synonymous with reliable timekeeping on the open water. With the rising popularity of wrist watches in the early twentieth century, UN adapted to the shift and carried much of what they had previously been known for into their wrist-bound timepieces. The piece that we have here is a chronograph dating to circa the 1930s, and what a beauty it is! The case measures approximately 33mm in diameter and features 'fixed' bar lugs, a flat 'pumpkin' crown, and an 'oval' pusher at the 2 o'clock position to operate all functions of the chronograph. The case itself is excellent, very nicely preserved with symmetrical proportions, sharp edges on the lug undersides, and shows normal wear from age with some light tooling marks. Inside, the stark white dial is almost entirely devoid of wear or patina, largely due to its porcelain composition. The surface has a recessed inner-circle with subsidiary registers that are recessed further still, a outer scale rendered in red, and stunning black printed 'Breguet' indices, minute markers, and UN text. The blued-steel 'syringe' handset ties it all together nicely and exhibits a light oxidation. It is powered by the Valjoux Cal. 22 — a robust and proven monopusher chronograph movement that found its way into a myriad of delightful chronographs in the first half of the twentieth century. Last but not least, this piece is accompanied by its inner box and serialized guarantee papers. An incredibly rare find for a watch thats pushing 100-years old. Even in the world of vintage, UN flies under the radar and remain largely overlooked. A shame, because if you dig deep enough into their catalog, there are absolute stunners to be found. This piece offers looks, pedigree, and presence that just exudes special. Thats because it is.

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 16014 - Grey 'Tapestry' Dial W/ Box & Papers
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The 4-Digit Datejusts was the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials — something that has stuck with the Datejust name ever since. What the 4-digits watches do lack, is a quickset date — something that was resolved with the introduction of the 5-digit pieces in the late 1970s. The piece that we have here, a Reference 16014 dates to circa 1978 and comes to us in fantastic overall condition. The case and matching Jubilee bracelet shows signs of very light previously polished and light signs of wear, with correct finishing present throughout. The characteristic 'fluted' white gold bezel has seemingly been spared of previous polishing and retains excellent definition and matching light wear. The dial within is exceptionally well-preserved and beautiful to behold. The grey surface features a 'tapestry' finishing with white text, applied indices, and gently patinated Tritium plots with a matching handset tying it all together. Of course, this piece also features a handy quickset date function. Last but not least, this piece comes accompanied by a inner box, outer box with a 16014 reference tag still present, COSC hangtag, and punched papers dating to 1979. All things considered, this is tough to beat, be it for your one vintage watch, or as an additional to a growing collection. Either way, these don't surface all too often and this is a fantastic example.

title: Benrus Type I Class A - Matte Black 'Sterile' Dial Military-Issued
description: Watches still played a critical role in military service in the 1970s. As a result of the need for a more robust dive watch tailored to the military's needs, the United States Department of Defense issued the MIL-W-50717 standard, which put forth a more robust list of required specifications, more so than any prior contract. There were many options for lower level officers and platoons when it came to timepieces, but for the best of the best including the renowned Navy Seals, the Benrus Type I and Type II were the best option. The Type I was the earliest version and notably more rare, making this piece one of only a handful ever produced. Benrus made these pieces exclusively for the military from 1972 to 1980, with this particular example dating to circa 1979 (April of 1979 to be exact). The 42.5mm asymmetrical case is one of the nicest that we have seen, offered in unpolished condition with excellent original 'parkerized' finishing and normal signs of wear. Flip it over, and the engravings on the caseback denoting it's military provenance and year of manufacture are crisp and clear. It even retains its original 'hash' marked screw-down crown. The bi-directional rotating bezel matches the condition of the case, with a very nicely-preserved black acrylic 12-hr insert. The matte black 'sterile' dial within shows only faint wear on the surface with evenly patinated Tritium elements and a matching white-painted handset. It comes with its original black single-pass nylon strap with PVD buckle. Due to their limited production, active use during military trials, decommissioning, and flat out loss, not all that many of these pieces survive today — particularly in this kind of condition. We are pleased to offer this Type I up for its next tour of duty, and invite you to strap a real piece of history to your wrist.

title: Breitling SuperOcean Ref. 1004 - Gloss Black Patina Dial Unpolished
description: Breitling has a long and rich history in chronographs — with an emphasis on aviation chronographs. And like so many other brands who have a watch model, or family that has become synonymous with the brand name itself, the Navitimer is just that for Breitling. As a result, the Navitimer casts a substantial shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the SuperOcean and Top Time ranges. The piece that we have here is the very first SuperOcean: the Ref. 1004. Conceived in the late 1950s as Breitling's answer to underwater timekeeping, these pieces never caught on quite like their contemporaries and remain incredible elusive. It is distinguished by its incredible attractive mid-century dial configuration with the bold 'broad arrow' handset, the wonderfully thin case, and the oversized concave bezel. The case itself measures 35mm in diameter but the bezel stretches another 4mm to 39mm in diameter, making for an excellent feel on the wrist. The glossy black dial with Radium is nicely preserved, showing minimal degradation and uniform patina compared other examples that have surfaced. The aforementioned 'Broad Arrow' handset shows some oxidation and matches nicely. The crown is signed and the engravings on the caseback remain clear and defined. The bezel shows normal wear and presents nicely. This piece comes fitted to period-correct stainless steel woven 'mesh' bracelet with a 'belt'-style buckle and is powered by Breitling's surprisingly thin, automatic-winding Cal. B125. Produced for only a few years and in extremely limited numbers, its not everyday a Ref. 1004 surfaces on the open market — let alone in strong condition like this example. This is a completely unique design coveted by enthusiast, dealers, and collectors alike and we're thrilled to be able to be offering this example.

title: Cartier Tank Louis Ref. 78086 - White Gold 'Paris' Dial
description: The Cartier Tank was one of the first wristwatches. Full stop! Inspired by the Renault Tanks used on the battlefield in WWI — yes, true story. Revolutionary at the time, Louis Cartier took inspiration from the profile of the treads on a period Renault tank, and based the case on them by way of the of brancards doubling as the lugs themselves. Over the course of the 20 th Century, the Tank became the watch to wear. Silent movie stars like Rudolph Valentino, artists like Andy Warhol, and even Jackie Kennedy were all fans of the signature timepiece from the King of Jewelers and the Jeweler of Kings. An icon indeed in the truest sense of the word. The model was first introduced in a few different case shapes which bore different names that intertwine with the inspiration behind them. Perhaps the most significant, well-known, and debatably desirable of these first pieces, the Tank Louis Cartier, was introduced in 1922 and was named after Louis Cartier himself. When people think of a Cartier Tank, theres a good change that this is the model that comes to mind. The example that we have here is one of those pieces. Dating to the early 1970s, it features the classically-sized 23mm x 31mm rectangular case that everyone loves, but rather than being crafted out of yellow gold, this example is of white gold. It comes to us in strong, nicely preserved overall condition, having been very lightly previously polished, with clear and defined hallmarks and correct factory proportions. It shows normal signs of wear and some sleeve-polish throughout from age and is devoid of any major damage. Inside, the white enamel 'Paris' signed dial inside retains its crisp white color and strong black printed text. When viewed under magnification, a faint and even 'crazing' is present throughout. Of course, it also features a blued-steel 'sword' handset, which is complimented by a blue sapphire cabochon winding crown at the 3 o'clock position. Last but not least, this example is accompanied by its period-correct Cartier signed white gold deployant clasp — a rare find! While production numbers are unclear, we probably see one white gold Tank for every twenty or so in yellow... This is a great opportunity to add what is not only a very uncommon Tank from this era, but a piece worthy of the iconic nomenclature that it bears to your collection.

title: Universal Genève Compur Ref. 22445 - Luminous Black Dial Unpolished
description: Universal Genève was one of the many great brands that succumbed to the quartz crisis of the 1970s. While they disappeared, it was not for their lack of impressive watches. To underscore that fact, keep in mind that Henri Stern Watch Agency in their nearly 80-year history has only ever sold two brands: Patek Philippe, and Universal Genève. The piece that we have here hails from the early 1940s — a time when the world was at war. Predating the more recognizable ‘Compax’ line of watches were a few different chronographs produced with specific use-cases in mind (e.g., Film-Compax, Medico-Compax, Dato-Compax, etc.) this 'Compur' chronograph was a relatively straightforward two-register chronograph in the family. Far simpler than their perhaps better known high complication ‘Tri-Compax,' the Compur were still offered with a variety of cases and dial variants and utilized in-house Universal Genève calibres. This particular Reference 22445 is amongst the finest we have ever seen. Dating to circa 1941, the 37mm stainless steel case remains in unpolished condition, with nice symmetrical lugs, square pushers, and a snapback caseback. Inside, unlike so many Compurs out there, this one not only features a stunning glossy black dial, but one in fantastic condition. Beautifully preserved throughout, the surface is largely clean and devoid of any major wear or moisture incursion, with excellent text, 'concentric' finishing within the subsidiary registers, attractive patinated numerals, and a beautifully matching 'kite' handset. This piece is powered by UG's manual-winding Cal. 287. Examples in condition like this with a desirable configuration simply do not surface on the open market all that often... and with the recent re-launch of the brand, collectors seem to be holding on to pieces like this, making for a great opportunity to grab this one.

title: Girard-Perregaux 'Mid Size' Chronograph Ref. 5070 - Silver 'Breguet' Dial Unpolished
description: Girard-Perregaux can trace its roots to 1791, when Jean-François Bautte began producing watches in Geneva, though the name we know came later. In 1856, Constant Girard married Marie Perregaux, and the two joined their surnames into a single company in La Chaux-de-Fonds. Girard-Perregaux wasn't chasing trends, but rather building a reputation on refined movements and serious technical ambition. That ambition produced one of the most iconic pieces in horology: the Tourbillon with Three Gold Bridges, patented by Constant Girard in 1884. It went on to win gold medals at the Paris Exposition Universelle in 1889, cementing the brand's standing among the elite Swiss manufacturers of the era. That is to say, GP has some real chops. Today, they are perhaps best known for the Laureato, the integrated-bracelet sports watch that has been revived in recent years and become a thoughtful alternative to some of the more sought-after pieces in the segment. Even in the world of vintage GP flies under the radar and remain largely overlooked. A shame, because if you dig deep enough into their catalog from the first half of the twentieth century, there are absolute stunners to be found. The piece that we have here is one such example, a chronograph dating to circa the 1940s. The 'mid size' case comes in at 30mm in diameter and remains in fantastic unpolished condition throughout. The flat bezel design, lugs, square pushers, and mid-case all retain crisp factory finishing and show just light wear given its age. The dial inside, however, is no doubt the highlight here... in equally fantastic condition, the silver surface shows only faint wear under magnification and features a two-register layout with stunning enamel 'Breguet' indices with a blued-steel 'feuille' handset tying everything together. As a cherry on top, the Calibre 281 movement powering this is sourced from another, prominent manufacturer of chronographs in this era: Universal Gevève. Even with its 30mm case diameter, this piece offers looks, pedigree, and presence that just exudes special. Thats because it is.

title: Longines 'Tre Tacche' Ref. 22243 - Black 'Gilt' Non-Luminous Dial
description: Longines is one of the most well respected manufacturers of the 20th century, full stop. Founded in 1832 in Saint-Imier, Switzerland, the company built a name for themselves early on as a manufacturer of quality in-house movements right from the start. Throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Longines also built a reputation for precision timekeeping, earning accolades at international exhibitions and becoming a trusted name in sports timing, particularly in horse racing and aviation — an association with continues until today. By the mid-20th century, especially from the 1930s to the 1960s, Longines was at the peak of its technical and aesthetic prowess, producing a range of high-grade wristwatches admired today by collectors and vintage enthusiasts. The brand was known for its beautifully finished in-house movements, such as the 13ZN and 30CH chronographs, which are considered some of the finest column-wheel chronographs ever produced. The piece that we have here is a simple, no-frills calatrava-style watch that has developed a cult following in the world of vintage Longines for its high-grade movement, robust case construction, and attractive, legible dial layouts. Known to collectors as a 'Tre-Tacche' for its distinct 'three notches' in the caseback, these pieces were available with a few case sizes, dial configurations, and even different time-only movements. This example features a non-luminous black dial within a 35mm stainless steel case; a very uncommon configuration. The case has bene previously polished and retains correct proportions with its distinct 'stepped' top-case, curved down lugs, and screw-down caseback. The black dial inside is nicely-preserved and shows light wear and signed of aging, with clear minute markers and 'Arabic' indices with a matching gold-tone 'pencil' handset. Powering this piece is Longines legendary manual-winding Calibre 12.68. The Tre-Tacche can best be described as an early tool watch. Almost like something of a predecessor to the Rolex Explorer, Omega Seamaster, etc. We feel that these day, Longines doesn't quite get the respect that they once had, making this a great time to grab a strong, honest example like this.

title: Audemars Piguet Yellow Gold 'Coin' Watch - Satin Silver Dial
description: The year 1972 was the advent of what is undeniably Audemars Piguet's most famous, significant, and yes, iconic line of watches, the Royal Oak. It was also the year that the 'high-end dress watch' would forever change. Prior to 1972, ultra-thin and design-focused precious metal watches represented the pinnacle of the genre, not what appears to be an industrial-styled stainless steel sports watch with a bracelet. While the brand never stopped producing traditional dress watches, per-se, production of their new golden goose would dominate the rest of the lineup. And this is after considering that prior to the Royal Oak, AP made far fewer watches to start with... That said, you may have noticed that this isn't a watch. So whats going on? What we have here is what is known as a 'coin watch' — a concept adopted a number of prominent brands in this era. These are generally made by using two gold coins, one for each side, with another watch case housed inside. Some were even produced with lugs and designed to be worn on a leather strap, but are the pieces like this one that almost perfectly resemble a coin that are the most interesting. This example, of course, is an AP. A good start! The yellow gold case comes in at 34mm in diameter, and features 'coin edge' finishing on the profile with a 'hidden' push button to open the closure at the 3 o'clock position. Once opened, the actual timepiece becomes visible and can be tilted up on a hinge by way of a tab at the 6 o'clock position. The crown at the 1 o'clock position then becomes usable to both wind and set the timepiece. The dial within is silver in color and has a satin finished surface, along with simple printed 'stick' indices and a matching blued-steel 'pencil' handset. Inside the watch case, the movement is an ultra-thin manually-would calibre. On top of being an obscure piece that is not immediately associated with AP, this watch — an 'object' really, is a glimpse into an era when subtlety and ultra-thin watchmaking rained supreme. The phrase 'if you know, you know' may never be more perfectly applied to a timepiece....

title: Lemania Monopusher Chronograph Ref. 0552/924-3312 - 'Brushed' Silver Non-Luminous Dial British Military Issued
description: Lemania can trace its roots back to the Vallée de Joux, where it was founded in 1884 by Alfred Lugrin, a former Jaeger-LeCoultre craftsman with a talent for complicated movements. Operating first under his own name, Lugrin built a modest but formidable reputation through his chronograph work before his son-in-law Marius Meylan took the reins around 1930 and renamed the company Lemania. Survival through the Great Depression came by joining forces with Omega and Tissot in 1932, and it was within the newly-formed alliance that Lemania's true legacy was forged: Every Omega chronograph movement for the next four decades, including the the iconic Calibre .321, would be supplied or closely based off Lemania calibres. The Quartz Crisis of the 1970s nearly unravelled it all, and by 1981 Lemania had separated from the group and reborn itself as Nouvelle Lemania. A decade later, Breguet brought it into the fold, and when the Swatch Group absorbed Breguet in 1999, the Lemania name was quietly retired — though its workshops now forming movements for Manufacture Breguet. The piece that we have here is a monopusher chronograph issued to the British Royal Navy for one very specific use-case. Like virtually every military-issued watch for decades prior be it a diver or for aviation, they were produced with luminous dials for legibility in generally low-light environments, at night, and for underwater use. In the 1970s, the luminous element of choice was Tritium, which while extremely low relative to its predecessor, Radium, does emit a radioactive signature. On nuclear-powered submarines, the worst case scenario is a reactor leak (see K19: The Widowmaker), so as a preventative measure, these subs had radiation detectors everywhere to monitor and ultimately prevent an almost certainly catastrophic event like a nuclear reactor meltdown. So, had the occupants been wearing watches with Tritium all over the dial and hands, the geiger readings would be completely inaccurate and constantly firing. Thats where this piece comes in, with a dial devoid of any radioactive material. Dating to circa the 1960s, this piece remains in strong overall condition given its past history. It features a wonderfully-sized 38mm case with a winding crown at the 3 o'clock position, a single 'pump' pusher at 2 o'clock, and a screw-down caseback with the appropriate military engravings. Inside, the silver dial retains excellent printed text and shows signs of a life lived with some aging and wear present on the surface and that desirable 'broad arrow' logo prominently featured on the lower half. The correct 'syringe' handset is the correct black-painted non-luminous set. Not only is this a piece of history, but when compared to other military-issued pieces from other brands, this actually is fantastic value, and they sure don't grow on trees!

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 1601  - 'Lavender' Dial W/ Papers
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The ‘4 digit’ series of Datejust are particularly attractive for their pie-pan dials which offer a layer of three-dimensionality to the dials that went away with the advent of quickset date and 5-digit Datejusts. These early Datejusts were available as the 1601, with a fluted white gold bezel, or the 1603, with an engine-turned steel bezel. The 4-Digit Datejusts were also the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials. This particular piece is a Reference 1601 from circa 1970 and it comes to us in fantastic overall condition. The case has been very gently and tastefully previously polished, retaining correct proportions and shows normal wear. The characteristic white gold 'fluted' bezel and the Jubilee bracelet have seemingly been spared of previous polishing and shows matching wear. Inside, this piece features a stunning and rare dial. Purple in color, it has a vibrant sunburst finishing with black printed text and applied indices and is seemingly devoid of any wear or inconsistencies. The Tritium plots remain fully intact and exhibit a rich and even patina throughout, with a nicely matching handset. Additionally, this piece is accompanied by punched guarantee papers. These Lavendar-dialed Datejusts are quite a bit rarer than you may think... We only see one or two per year, so don't miss out on this fantastic example.

title: Universal Genève Compax Ref. 12558 - Patinated Pink Dial
description: Universal Genève was one of the many great brands that succumbed to the quartz crisis of the 1970s. While they disappeared, it was not for their lack of impressive watches. To underscore that fact, keep in mind that Henri Stern Watch Agency in their nearly 80-year history has only ever sold two brands: Patek Philippe, and Universal Genève. Far simpler than their perhaps more well-known high complication ‘Tri-Compax,' this piece comes from the long-running family of 'Compax' watches, which it shares its name with. Some of which were produced with specific use-cases in mind (e.g., Film-Compax, Medico-Compax, Dato-Compax, etc.), in different metals, sizes, etc., with this piece being a relatively straightforward three-register chronograph. The example that we have here is Ref. 12558 dating to circa 1945. It features a very desirable pink-on-pink configuration, with a rose gold case and pink dial within. More on that later. The case measures approximately 36mm in diameter and features subtle but thoughtful facets on the lugs, with beautiful brushed profiles, square pushers, and a a polished rose gold bezel. Inside, the pink dial possesses a matte surface with applied 'dot' indices and 'concentric' subsidiary registers. The surface has developed a light and uniform patina from age, no resembling more of a warm taupe tone. The indices also show oxidation when inspected closely and the rose gold-tone handset with blued-steel chronograph hands match wonderfully. It is powered by UG's Cal. 287 manual-winding movement, which is tucked behind a snapback caseback with deep and clear engravings. Examples in condition like this with a desirable configuration simply do not surface on the open market all that often... and with the recent re-launch of the brand, collectors seem to be holding on to pieces like this, making for a great opportunity to grab this one.

title: Rolex Day-Date Ref. 1803/9 - Sunburst Silver 'Door Stop' Dial
description: When the Day-Date was released in 1956, Rolex had made numerous attempts to capture the market with more complicated timepieces such as the Ref. 6036, the Ref. 8171, and the Ref. 6062, but it seemed like buyers were not particularly fond of complicated Rolexes. All of that changed when President Lyndon B. Johnson was spotted wearing one Rolex in particular: a Day-Date. The model has since become known worldwide as ‘The President’ and as a symbol of success and prestige. Simply put, this one stuck. The Day-Date was available for many years on a matching solid gold bracelet (called a 'President' bracelet), but also on a leather strap like the example that we have here. This Reference 1803 dates to circa 1966 and is constructed out of solid white gold. It comes to us with a strong, gently previously polished case with a correct 'fluted' white gold bezel, and even an original white gold crown. Inside, the silver dial remains in simply fantastic condition, with a vibrant sunburst surface and applied indices with 'door stop' indices at the 6 & 9 o'clock positions. Especially when fitted to a leather strap, this 'elevated' piece remains very much under-the-radar. If you know, you know.

title: Rolex Oysterquartz Day-Date Ref. 19018 - Sunburst Champagne Dial W/ Box & Papers
description: The 1970s were an interesting time for the watch industry. The Great Quartz Crisis from Japan offered the world better quality watches, that were more accurate, more reliable, and generally much more affordable. A kiss of death for mechanical watchmaking at the time. Even the very best of Switzerland will still lose accuracy over time — an issue that a quartz watch virtually solved (though not perfect). Great, beloved Swiss brands like Universal Genève, Gallet, Zodiac, and Blancpain would disappear — some of which were acquired by holding companies, other brands, etc. and eventually resurface, but hundreds of smaller brands were completely wiped away. Rolex responded by producing their own version of the quartz watch called it the Oysterquartz, which introduced a more style-forward and angular design that was becoming popular in the 1970s, and of course, a quartz movement inside. On top of this new model line name, these pieces utilized existing cornerstone model names to denote specific models with the Oysterquartz range, such as the Datejust and Day-Date. By the middle of the 1980s, the Swiss watch industry was able to pivot and re-establish itself as a luxury product worthy of higher prices that could justify the cost and complexity of designing and manufacturing a mechanical watch. So, the Oysterquartz is massively important in the history of Rolex, representing the only time in its nearly 120-years of business that it was ever under siege in a truly threatening way. These did not stay in the Rolex lineup for long and are therefore surprisingly unusual to come by. The piece that we have here is a Day-Date variant dating to circa 1978, and as with all other pieces in Rolex's flagship line, it is constructed out of solid gold. Inside, it has a classic, sunburst champagne dial with applied indices and both day and date apertures. The case and integrated bracelet are in fantastic overall condition and showing normal signs of wear throughout with visible factory finishing. The characteristic 'fluted' yellow gold bezel retains crisp finishing and also shows normal signs of wear. Inside, the dial is crisp and vibrant and is seemingly devoid of any wear or damage on the surface. The Tritium plots are evenly patinated and complimented perfectly by a matching handset. Additionally, this piece is accompanied by its inner ad outer boxes, booklets, and papers. This then, is a strange yet important piece from the pages of Rolex's history, and is a must if you are looking to add a Day-Date to a collection of many, or simply snag a lesser-known piece thats a bit out of the ordinary.

title: Tudor Submariner Date Ref. 76100 - Blue Dial Unpolished W/ Papers
description: The Submariner, namely those produced by Rolex, has long been considered the cream of the crop when it comes to watch collecting as a whole. Possibly the most iconic watch ever produced, the Submariner has long standing utilitarian roots that span decades, and everyone who’s anyone has been spotted wearing one. However, if you look deeper into the Submariner line, you may find a less known but just as incredible model manufactured by Tudor. These pieces are not only more unique and rare than the traditional Submariner, but offer much greater value. Designed as a replacement for the quintessential Tudor ‘Snowflake’ Submariners, the References 76100 and 79090 is in many collectors eyes, the last great vintage Tudor Submariner. These pieces all had matte dials with Tritium plots and matching Tritium-filled handsets, cases with lug-holes, acrylic crystals, and folded-link Oyster bracelets. In many ways, This is all stuff that we see in Rolex and Tudor models as early as the 1960s, but were produced well-into the 1990s! The example that we have here dates to circa 1987 and remains in fantastic overall condition. The case remains unpolished, with clear factory finishing visible throughout and shows normal wear from age. The bezel also remains unpolished, with strong knurling and houses a gorgeous faded blue insert. Inside, it features a desirable blue dial, which retains a rich deep blue color with gently patinated Tritium indices and a matching handset. It comes fitted to its correct steel Oyster bracelet with a Rolex-signed fliplock clasp. Additionally, this piece is accompanied by papers. These Tudor Subs of the mid 1980s into the mid 1990s not only present great value next to their Rolex cousins, but are very interesting in that they offer nearly all the feel of a Rolex Submariner Date dating back to the 1960s — with the charm of an acrylic crystal, a matte dial, and even a folded-link bracelet — for only a fraction of the entry cost. And Rolex sure never made a steel Submariner with a blue dial!

title: Breitling Duograph Ref. 766 'Rattrapante' - Silver Patina Dial
description: Breitling has a long and rich history in chronographs — with an emphasis on aviation chronographs. And like so many other brands who have a watch model, or family that has become synonymous with the brand name itself, the Navitimer is just that for Breitling. As a result, the Navitimer casts a substantial shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the SuperOcean, Top Time, and lesser-known pieces that pre-date model ranges all together. The piece that we have here is one of the latter. The 1940s was a time when Breitling was rapidly expanding their chronograph offerings, and the Duograph represented a significant step forward for the manufacture, combining the elegant proportions of the period with one of the most sophisticated complications available at the time: the split-seconds, or 'rattrapante,' chronograph. Like many of Breitling’s chronographs from this period, the Duograph was offered in both steel and precious metals, with variations in case design, pushers, and dial configurations adding further character to an already elusive model. The example that we have here Ref. 766 dating to circa 1951 and is offered in strong overall condition. The case comes in at 35mm and features gorgeous, prominent 'stepped' lugs, square pushers, a snapback caseback, and a crown at 3 o'clock that functions as the split-seconds activation in addition to winding and setting the movement. Inside, the silver dial has aged to show an attractive and largely uniform patina, while retaining clear printing throughout with patinated indices and a nicely matching blued-steel handset. Powering this piece is the highly-complex Venus Caliber 185, which incorporate both the split-seconds function and a three-register design, all in a form that is no larger than that of a typical chronograph from the era. Even today, a remarkable achievement. As it pertains to vintage collecting, it is precisely this combination of rarity, mechanical complexity, and unmistakable 1940s design language that makes a Duograph such a compelling timepiece, full stop.

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 1601 - Matte Black Dial
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The ‘4 digit’ series of Datejust are particularly attractive for their pie-pan dials which offer a layer of three-dimensionality to the dials that went away with the advent of quickset date and 5-digit Datejusts. These early Datejusts were available as the 1601, with a fluted white gold bezel, or the 1603, with an engine-turned steel bezel. The 4-Digit Datejusts were also the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials. This particular piece is a Reference 1601 from circa 1972 and it comes to us in strong overall condition. The case retains symmetrical proportions at all four concerns and shows normal signs of wear throughout. The characteristic 'fluted' white gold bezel shows matching wear and retains its 'fluted' finishing. Inside, the black dial shows some is largely clean and presents nicely, with crisp silver text, fully-intact Tritium plots, and a matching handset. It comes fitted to a period correct 'oval'-link Jubilee bracelet with a signed blade clasp. All things considered, be it for your one vintage watch, or as an additional to a growing collection, this is a great example.

title: Rolex Antimagnetic Chronograph Ref. 3233 - Silver Patina Dial
description: The Rolex Daytona has long been one of the most desirable chronographs in production, which is funny for a model that was initially off to a slow sales start! …but this comes before all of that! Predating even what are known as ‘Pre-Daytonas' are the non Oyster-style case chronographs. Produced from roughly the 1930s through the 1940s, these chronographs generally utilize a snapback case with a wide variety of lug designs, silver or black dials with numerous handsets, and two-register layouts. The piece that we have here is simply known as an Antimagnetic Chronograph. It features a 35mm case with 'oval' pushers, a beautiful 'onion' crown, and 'hinged' lugs. Inside, the white dial has developed a very attractive and largely even 'toasted' patina across the satin surface, while retains excellent black printing with a telemetré scale on the outside edge and a black-painted handset. It is powered by a manual-winding chronograph movement with a Rolex-signed bridge. The 1930s-1950s are an era where Rolex was not yet the big guy on the scene. The brad was still figuring out what works and what would stick, so there is a huge variety of designs to be discovered that can seem almost unique. This piece embodies that belief, and for far, far less than a steel Daytona produced in much greater numbers.

title: Rolex Day-Date Ref. 1803 - Sunburst Champagne Dial Unpolished
description: When the Day-Date was released in 1956, Rolex had made numerous attempts to capture the market with more complicated timepieces such as the Ref. 6036, the Ref. 8171, and the Ref. 6062, but it seemed like buyers were not particularly fond of complicated Rolexes. All of that changed when President Dwight D. Eisenhower was spotted wearing one Rolex in particular: a Day-Date. The model has since become known worldwide as ‘The President’ and as a symbol of success and prestige. Simply put, this one stuck. The Day-Date was available for many years on a leather strap with a matching gold buckle, but also on a solid gold bracelet (called a 'President' bracelet), like the example that we have here. The Reference 1803 that we have here dates to circa 1974 and comes to us in excellent overall condition. The case, characteristic 'fluted' yellow gold bezel, and 'President' bracelet all remain unpolished and show matching normal wear throughout. The 'champagne' dial within features a sunburst finishing is beautifully preserved, with fully-intact and evenly patinated Tritium plots and a perfectly matching handset. The 'President' bracelet is fitted with a 'hidden' clasp and bears a few rare stamps indicating that it was originally for the South American market. This is a fantastic example of an icon, full stop.

title: Cartier Cristallor Ref. 78096 - White Enamel 'Paris' Dial
description: Cartier's catalog is full of pieces that don't bear "Tank" in front of the model name, and many remain overlooked or flat out unknown to the vast majority of consumers. Introduced in 1973 as a part of the Louis Cartier Collection, the Cristallor is a textbook example of one such model. Produced in a handful of variants over the years, in a number of different metals, sizes, and with different movements, this is another gorgeous execution of Cartiers ubiquitous design language. The piece that we have here is an early example from circa the early 1970s. The solid yellow gold case comes in at 28mm x 34mm and features a hexagonal 'stepped' design with 'hidden' lugs, a sapphire cabochon crown, and a manual-winding movement within. The dial inside is exactly what you'd expect to find from Cartier during this era, with a white enamel surface, printed black 'Roman' indices with an inner chemin de fer minute track. Of course, everything is tied together with a blued-steel 'sword' handset. If nothing from the Tank or Santos family speaks to you, this might just be a perfect alternative, and quite a bit more rare.

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 1603 - Sunburst Grey 'Sigma' Dial
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The ‘4 digit’ series of Datejust are particularly attractive for their pie-pan dials which offer a layer of three-dimensionality to the dials that went away with the advent of quickset date and 5-digit Datejusts. These early Datejusts were available as the 1601, with a fluted white gold bezel, or the 1603, with an engine-turned steel bezel. The 4-Digit Datejusts were also the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials. This particular piece is a Reference 1603 from circa 1972 and it comes to us in strong overall condition, with a gently previously polished case, an 'engine-turned' steel bezel, and a matching Jubilee bracelet — all showing uniform normal wear. Inside, the sunburst grey 'Sigma' dial is beautifully preserved, retaining a crisp and vibrant sunburst finishing seemingly devoid of the usual degradation found on colored dials from this era. The Tritium plots remain fully-intact and show an attractive and even patina throughout with a handset that has ages a bit darker. All things considered, this is tough to beat, be it for your one vintage watch, or as an additional to a growing collection.

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 16014 - Black Dial
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The 4-Digit Datejusts was the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials — something that has stuck with the Datejust name ever since. What the 4-digits watches do lack, is a quickset date — something that was resolved with the introduction of the 5-digit pieces in the late 1970s. The piece that we have here, a Reference 16014 from circa 1982, comes to us with an excellent, gently and tastefully previously polished Oyster case with the correct 'fluted' white gold bezel seemingly spared of previous polished. Inside, the black dial presents nicely, with a deep glossy surface and evenly patinated Tritium plots with a matching handset. Of course, this piece also features a handy quickset date function and comes fitted to a correct solid-link Jubilee bracelet with a signed blade clasp. Black-dialed Datejusts are less common than you may think... And there is almost some Explorer-like sportiness about them, while of course, still being a Datejust. This one, like virtually any Datejust , can be your one vintage watch, or as an additional to a growing collection.

title: Rolex King Midas Ref. 4315 - 'Brushed' Champagne Dial W/ Hangtag
description: In the late 1960s, Rolex was looking to expand their lineup of watches with both more traditional designs, as well as design-forward offerings. This line of watches became known called the Cellini line with a subsidiary lineup called 'Midas.' Like the rest of the Cellini line, the Midas pieces would come in a wide variety of shapes, sizes, and dial options, and all in solid gold. The flagship offering within the Midas line, the 'King Midas' were amongst the most expensive models the brand had ever produced and, at the time, limited in their production. The piece that we have here is one of those watches, a King Midas Reference 4315. This very special piece features a five-sided case with a screw-down caseback, "King Midas" engraved into the left case profile, a truly integrated 'flat-link' bracelet with a 'hidden' deployant clasp, and a recessed crown at the 9 o'clock position styled to look like a sun. This particular yellow gold example dates to circa 1976 and is offered in excellent overall condition. The case and bracelet both show normal signs of wear from age with no notable damage or blemishes and no 'stretch.' The dial within features a 'brushed' texture on the champagne dial with an applied coronet logo, Cellini script on the bottom half, and a simple yellow gold stick handset. Most of the Cellini family features manual-winding movements, and this piece is no different. This then, is a brilliant example of Rolex displaying a more artistic side, all while very much being a Rolex at heart. Low production, precious materials, and its a Rolex. Hard to beat.

title: Omega 6B/542 Ref. 2777-1 - Matte Black 'Fat Arrow' Dial RAF-Issued Unpolished
description: Omega is undeniably one of the most historically important timepiece manufactures of all time. In fact, the Speedmaster is probably the most important wrist watch of all time. As a result, the Speedmaster casts a massive shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the Seamaster and Constellation ranges. The resulting effect is double sided: many vintage Omegas, we feel are incredibly undervalued in the market as it exists today, with the other side of that being that hidden gems are shocking attainable. The piece that we have here is special for a multitude of reasons. Not dissimilar to the 'Dirty Dozen' watches of WWII, this piece was commissioned by the British Ministry Of Defence to produce a watch that met a series of standards. Omega, along with a handful of other prominent watch manufacturers would rise to the challenge to produce a timepiece that had a certain level of resistance to shock, magnetism, dust, and of course, excellent timekeeping. Dating to circa 1953, this example is offered in fantastic overall condition. The 36mm case remains unpolished and shows normal wear with no notable damage or indication this ever really saw the action that it was intended... It features 'fixed' lug bars and a screw-down caseback with all of the correct engravings. No doubt the most intriguing element of the condition on this piece, is the dial. As a general rule with military watches, hands and dials were replaces under contract service, and as a result is accepted in the collector community. The result is that many military-issued piece prior to the 1960s no longer have their original dials with Radium paint, rather later dials with Tritium (this is where the 'Circle T' comes from). With the 6B/542, however, rather than a 'circle T' the MOD choose to denote the presence of Tritium on the new dials with a thicker 'fat' Broad Arrow. The dial itself presents nicely, showing light wear throughout with clear printing and evenly patinated Tritium elements and a correct Tritium 'sword' handset. This piece comes fitted to a very appropriate Admiralty Grey NATO strap from Phoenix and is powered by Omegas Cal. 283 manual-winding movement. Rumored to have only been produced for a year or two, there's no saying how many examples survive today, let alone in condition as well-rounded as this. To many collectors of vintage, regardless of whether the focus is of military watches or not, this piece has everything going for it. Military issued, properly vintage, and its from one of the most storied brands in the history of watchmaking. This is a real piece of history — a phrase often repeated in the world of watches, though rarely as deservedly as in this case.

title: Tudor Submariner Ref. 7928 'PCG' - Gilt 'Tropical' Dial
description: The Submariner, namely those produced by Rolex, has long been considered the cream of the crop when it comes to watch collecting as a whole. Possibly the most iconic watch ever produced, the Submariner has long standing utilitarian roots that span decades, and everyone who’s anyone has been spotted wearing one. However, if you look deeper into the Submariner line, you may find a less known but just as incredible model manufactured by Tudor. The Ref. 7928 that we have here dates to circa 1961 and is offered in strong overall condition. The case remains thick and symmetrical, with the 'pointed crown guards' clearly on display and factory chamfers visible. Inside, the glossy black 'gilt' dial has aged to various shades of brown, resulting in a wildly tropical patina. The luminous plots also shows patina from age and are complimented by a matching handset. The knurled bezel houses an excellent black 'fat font' insert with a patinated pip and it comes fitted to a slightly later 'stretch-rivet' Oyster bracelet with a blade clasp. For many of us, this is what vintage is all about: subtle details, honest condition that tells a story, and uniqueness in wear/patina. This one embodies all of the above!

title: Vacheron Constantin Rectangular Dress Watch Ref. 7139 - 'Brushed' Silver Dial
description: Vacheron Constantin can trace its roots back to 1755 and along with only a handful of other brands, is credited as one of the oldest manufacturers of mechanical clocks, pocket-watches, and of course, watches. In fact, Vacheron enjoys the prestige as the oldest continually operating manufacturer that still operates today. Vacheron is also a member of what has become known as The Holy Trinity , along with Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet. All three of these manufactures have very different identities and focus areas within the industry, with VC generally regarded as the technical innovator. And despite a bevy of both technical and mechanical firsts, including the most complicated watch ever at the time of writing this, VC remains the lesser known name of the three in the broader watch community and certainly least understood. The piece that we have here is a yellow gold rectangular dress watch dating to circa 1960. The case comes in at 19mm x 29mm and remains in excellent condition, showing just normal wear with a gentle warmth to the gold. The dial inside is silver in color and features an elegant, vertically 'brushed' finishing with applied indices and is complimented by a matching 'pencil' handset. It comes fitted to a signed black alligator strap with a gold tone buckle and is powered by Vacheron's Calibre K1001/2 manual-winding movement. In some ways, this piece is very different for Vacheron. Highly restrained when it comes to eccentric, daring details and 'simple' in its design. That of course means, like other Swiss watches from this era, the execution and simplicity speaks for itself.

title: Audemars Piguet 'Hinged-Lug' Dress Watch - Satin Silver Dial W/ Box
description: The year 1972 was the advent of what is undeniably Audemars Piguet's most famous, significant, and yes, iconic line of watches, the Royal Oak. It was also the year that the 'high-end dress watch' would forever change. Prior to 1972, ultra-thin and design-focused precious metal watches represented the pinnacle of the genre, not what appears to be an industrial-styled stainless steel sports watch with a bracelet. While the brand never stopped producing traditional dress watches, per-se, production of their new golden goose would dominate the rest of the lineup. So, watches like the svelte and, frankly, stunning yellow gold dress watch that we have here offer offer not just a ton of value next to their iconic siblings, but were produced in relatively limited quantities. The piece that we have here is one of those pre-Royal Oak era watches: a rare yellow gold 'Tank'-style dress watch dating to circa the 1950s. Noticeable even at a glance, the lugs hint at their fully-articulating nature, with fine spacing between them and the case itself. When turned to profile view, the articulating nature of the lugs becomes apparent, as well as the intricate, sculpted finishing that they possess throughout. The bezel has a high-polish finish, framing the satin silver dial within. The dial itself shows honest signs of aging, with applied yellow gold 'dart' and 'Arabic' indices, a subsidiary seconds register on the lower half, and a yellow gold 'pencil' handset typing it all together. It is powered by a manual-winding movement by AP. Last but not least, this piece is accompanied by its box and comes fitted with a 'Saffiano'-textured brown leather strap with its original yellow gold signed buckle. This then, is a representation of a bygone era not just for Audemars Piguet, but for what a high-end dress watch used to be. Only in the last few years have collectors and enthusiasts alike started to pay a bit more attention to pieces like these and, we think, its long overdue.

title: Abercrombie & Fitch Co. Seafarer Ref. 2443 'Second Execution' - Silver Dial Unpolished
description: Abercrombie & Fitch Co., long before its modern reinvention, was one of America’s preeminent sporting outfitters. From its midtown Manhattan flagship, the firm supplied serious outdoorsmen with the finest equipment available, often commissioning bespoke products from respected manufacturers to meet the specific demands of its clientele. Watches were no exception. By the mid-20th century, A&F had begun offering co-branded timepieces tailored to sportsmen, and when customers began requesting a watch capable of tracking the tides, the company turned to one Charles-Edouard Heuer to bring the idea to life. Commissioned at A&F’s request, the Solunar was introduced in 1949 and advertised as the only watch to display both 'Solar' and 'Lunar' time. Produced in a limited run of just around 1,000 pieces, it was a highly specialized instrument and ultimately a niche offering. Still, its innovation laid the groundwork for the Seafarer, which paired the original tidal display with one of Heuer’s signature complications: the chronograph. Retaining traditional hour and minute counters, the Seafarer replaced the running seconds register with a tide indicator at 9 o’clock, which was directly adjustable via a left-side pusher and synchronized using published tide tables. Produced from the 1950s through the 1970s in several case configurations shared with other Heuer chronographs, the Seafarer remained a distinctive but specialized entry within the broader catalog and saw a handful of different variations over that time. The example that we have here, a Ref. 2443, dates to the 1950s and is offered in excellent, beautifully-preserved condition. The case comes in at 38mm in diameter and features nice thick lugs with sharp undersides, along with small 'pump' pushers, and a 'stepped' top case. Inside, the silver dial shows light aging throughout, retaining nice colors in within the subsidiary registers and beautiful gold 'foil' indices with a correct gold-tone handset. The movement powering this piece is a modified version of the famous Valjoux 72 which of course, is manually-wound. For the most part, all Abercrombie & Fitch Co. timepieces have become collectible to an extent, but it is the Seafarer that is at the front of the pack in both desirability and collectability. This is the first time we have had the pleasure of offering on for sale on the website and we could not be more happy about it.

title: Audemars Piguet White Gold Dress Watch Ref. 5259 - Silver Dial w/ Box & Papers
